UPDATE course_lessons SET content = '# Industrial Robot Types, Axes & Applications

## The Maintenance Technician''s Role with Robots

Industrial robots are no longer exotic — they are standard equipment in automotive, food processing, packaging, and logistics facilities. As a maintenance technician, you will not program robots from scratch, but you WILL:

- Recover from faults and alarms
- Replace failed components (motors, encoders, cables)
- Perform preventive maintenance (grease, battery replacement, backup)
- Troubleshoot communication between robots and PLCs
- Verify safety system integration after modifications

Understanding robot fundamentals is essential for all of these tasks.

## Robot Configurations

### Articulated (6-Axis) Robots

The most common industrial robot. Six rotary joints give complete freedom of movement — the robot can reach any point in its workspace from any angle.

**Axis layout:**

| Axis | Joint Type | Motion | Typical Motor |
|------|-----------|--------|---------------|
| J1 | Base rotation | Rotates entire robot left/right | AC servo, largest |
| J2 | Shoulder | Raises/lowers upper arm | AC servo, high torque |
| J3 | Elbow | Extends/retracts forearm | AC servo |
| J4 | Wrist roll | Rotates wrist inline | AC servo, smaller |
| J5 | Wrist pitch | Tilts wrist up/down | AC servo |
| J6 | Wrist yaw/flange | Rotates tool mounting flange | AC servo, smallest |

**Applications:** Welding, painting, assembly, machine tending, palletizing

**Key manufacturers:** FANUC (yellow), ABB (orange/white), KUKA (orange), Yaskawa/Motoman (blue)

### SCARA Robots (4-Axis)

Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm — fast, precise, and rigid in the vertical direction but compliant (flexible) in the horizontal plane.

**Characteristics:**
- 4 axes: 2 rotary (shoulder + elbow), 1 linear (Z up/down), 1 rotary (tool rotation)
- Extremely fast cycle times (0.3-0.5 seconds per pick)
- High repeatability (±0.01mm typical)
- Limited workspace compared to 6-axis

**Applications:** Electronics assembly, pick-and-place, screw driving, small part insertion

### Delta (Parallel) Robots

Three or four arms connected in parallel from a fixed overhead platform to a moving end-effector. Designed for extremely high-speed, lightweight picking.

**Characteristics:**
- 3-4 axes with parallel kinematic structure
- Speeds up to 10m/s, accelerations up to 15G
- Low payload (typically 0.5-8 kg)
- Mounted overhead (ceiling/gantry)

**Applications:** Food packaging, pharmaceutical sorting, small part picking at 150+ picks/minute

### Cartesian/Gantry Robots

Linear axes (X, Y, Z) arranged perpendicular to each other. Simple, rigid, and easy to size for large workspaces.

**Characteristics:**
- 3 linear axes + optional rotary wrist
- Workspace defined by rail lengths (can be very large)
- High payload capacity relative to cost
- Easy to understand and troubleshoot

**Applications:** CNC loading, palletizing large items, dispensing, 3D printing

### Collaborative Robots (Cobots)

Designed to work alongside humans without traditional safety fencing. Use force/torque sensors and compliant joints to detect contact and stop.

**Key safety features:**
- Force-limited joints (typically <150N contact force)
- Rounded surfaces, no pinch points
- Speed-limited when humans are nearby
- Power and force limiting per ISO/TS 15066

> **Important:** Cobots are NOT inherently safe. The end-of-arm tooling (gripper, tool) must also be assessed. A cobot holding a sharp knife is still dangerous. Risk assessment per ISO 10218-2 is always required.

## Robot Specifications: What the Numbers Mean

| Specification | What It Means | Why It Matters |
|--------------|---------------|----------------|
| Payload | Maximum weight at wrist flange (including tooling) | Exceeding causes servo faults, reduced life |
| Reach | Maximum distance from base to tool center point | Determines if robot can reach all positions |
| Repeatability | How precisely it returns to a taught point | ±0.02mm typical for spot welding |
| Axes/DOF | Number of independent motion axes | 6 = full flexibility, 4 = limited orientation |
| Speed | Maximum TCP (tool center point) velocity | Affects cycle time calculations |
| IP Rating | Ingress protection (dust/water) | IP67 required for washdown environments |
| Mounting | Floor, ceiling, wall, or angle | Affects reach envelope and workspace |

> **Technician Tip:** When a robot faults on "overload" or "excess torque" during a program that previously worked fine, check: (1) Is the payload correct? Did someone add a heavier tool? (2) Are the tool center point (TCP) parameters correct? Wrong TCP = wrong torque calculations. (3) Is a joint binding mechanically? Check for grease degradation or bearing wear.

## Robot Controller Architecture

Every industrial robot has these components:

**1. Controller Cabinet**
- Main CPU board (motion planning, program execution)
- Servo amplifiers (one per axis — converts position commands to motor current)
- Power supply (converts facility power to DC bus for servos)
- I/O boards (digital and analog interface to external equipment)
- Safety board (monitors E-stop, safety fences, enable switches)
- Teach pendant port

**2. Manipulator (Arm)**
- AC servo motors with brakes (one per axis)
- Absolute encoders (track position even when powered off — battery-backed)
- Reduction gears (harmonic drives or cycloidal reducers)
- Cables routed through arm (motor power, encoder feedback, tool signals)

**3. Teach Pendant**
- Handheld programming/operation device
- Deadman switch (3-position enabling device)
- Emergency stop button
- Jogging controls (move robot manually)
- Program display and editing

## Encoder Batteries: The Silent Killer

Absolute encoders track robot position using battery-backed memory. When batteries die:

1. Robot loses position reference (mastering is lost)
2. ALL programs become invalid until re-mastered
3. Re-mastering requires specialized fixtures or procedures
4. Downtime: 2-8 hours depending on robot and method

**PM requirement:** Replace encoder batteries every 1-2 years (or when low-battery alarm appears). NEVER let batteries die completely.

| Manufacturer | Battery Type | Location | Replacement Interval |
|-------------|-------------|----------|---------------------|
| FANUC | CR-17335 (3V lithium) | Controller backplane | 1 year (with power ON) |
| ABB | 3HAC16831 | SMB board in arm | 2 years |
| KUKA | 00-174-902 | Controller | 2 years |
| Yaskawa | HW0470360-A | Controller | 1.5 years |

> **Critical:** On FANUC robots, batteries MUST be replaced with the controller powered ON. If you replace them with power OFF, position data is lost immediately.

## Safety Integration

Robots are the most dangerous machines in a facility. Safety system integration is governed by:

- **ISO 10218-1** — Robot design requirements
- **ISO 10218-2** — Robot system integration requirements
- **ISO/TS 15066** — Collaborative robot safety (force limits)
- **ANSI/RIA 15.06** — North American robot safety standard

**Minimum safety requirements:**
1. Perimeter guarding (fence, light curtains, or safety scanners)
2. Interlocked access gates (safety-rated, monitored)
3. Emergency stop accessible from all operator positions
4. Enabling device (deadman switch) for teach mode
5. Reduced speed in teach mode (250mm/s maximum per ISO 10218)

## Knowledge Check

**Scenario:** A FANUC M-20iA (6-axis, 20kg payload) is used for machine tending. After a weekend shutdown, the robot displays "SRVO-062 BZAL alarm (Group 1, Axis 2)" and will not move. What does this mean and what is the recovery procedure?

**Answer:** SRVO-062 is a "Pulse coder battery alarm" — the encoder backup battery for Axis 2 (shoulder) is low or dead. If the alarm appeared while the robot was powered on, position data is likely still intact. Replace the battery immediately (with power ON), then clear the alarm. If position was lost, the robot requires re-mastering of Axis 2 using the mastering fixture or zero-position marks before any programs can run.' WHERE id = 90007;
